In these guidelines and other related documents, cases of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) and rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (RR-TB) are often grouped together under the term MDR/RR-TB. These cases are eligible for treatment using an MDR-TB regimen. 2. Rifampicin-susceptible, isoniazid-resistant tuberculosis refers to tuberculosis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains that are resistant to isoniazid but remain susceptible to rifampicin. 3. A serious adverse event is defined as an adverse event that can result in death, a life-threatening experience, hospitalization or prolonged hospitalization, persistent or significant disability, or a congenital anomaly. Events that do not immediately lead to these outcomes but require intervention to prevent them are also included. Such events may necessitate drastic measures, such as discontinuing the suspected medication. 4. Severe extrapulmonary tuberculosis includes conditions such as miliary (disseminated) TB or TB meningitis. In children and young adolescents under 15 years of age, extrapulmonary forms of TB other than lymphadenopathy (e.g., peripheral nodes or isolated mediastinal mass without compression) are considered severe. 5. Following a WHO expert consultation in September 2021, intrathoracic lymph node TB in children is now classified as pulmonary TB. 6. The Pocket Book of Hospital Care for Children provides guidelines for managing common childhood illnesses, including TB, and was last accessed on September 27, 2021. 7. A source case refers to an individual with active TB disease who has transmitted the infection to others in a new setting. This could be the index patient or another unidentified individual. 8. Systematic screening for TB disease involves identifying individuals at risk within a predetermined target group by assessing symptoms and using diagnostic tests or procedures that can be applied rapidly. For those who screen positive, the diagnosis must be confirmed through additional tests and clinical assessments. This term is sometimes used interchangeably with active TB case-finding but should be distinguished from testing for TB infection (e.g., TB skin test or interferon-gamma release assay). 9. The tuberculin skin test (TST) involves intradermal injection of mycobacterial antigens to elicit an immune response, represented by induration, which is measured in millimeters. TST is used to diagnose TB infection. 10. Tuberculosis (TB) refers to the disease state caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. In this handbook, it is commonly referred to as TB disease to differentiate it from TB infection. 11. TB infection is defined as a state of persistent immune response to stimulation by Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens without evidence of clinically manifest TB disease. This term replaces the previously used latent TB infection. There is no gold standard test for directly identifying M. tuberculosis infection in humans. Most infected individuals show no signs or symptoms of TB but remain at risk of developing TB disease. 12. Tuberculosis preventive treatment (TPT) is offered to individuals at risk of developing TB disease to reduce that risk. It is also referred to as treatment of TB infection or TB preventive therapy. 13. Among children under 10 years of age, malnutrition is often defined as a weight-for-age Z-score below -2 standard deviations. 14. Children and adolescents under 15 years of age represent approximately 11% of all TB cases globally, with an estimated 1 million children and young adolescents falling ill with TB each year. However, less than half of these cases are notified by national TB programs, leading to a significant gap in case detection, particularly among children under 5 years of age. 15. Challenges contributing to this gap include difficulties in specimen collection and bacteriological confirmation of TB in young children due to the paucibacillary nature of TB in this age group and the lack of highly sensitive point-of-care diagnostic tests. 16. Children and adolescents typically access primary health care or child health services, where the capacity to recognize presumptive TB and access diagnostic services is often limited. 17. In 2020, only one-third of child contacts under 5 years of age eligible for TPT actually received it. 18. Adolescents, particularly those aged 15–19 years, are also significantly affected by TB, with an estimated half a million cases globally each year. Unlike young children, adolescents are an important risk group for TB transmission due to the infectiousness of their disease and their high social mobility. 19. The WHO operational handbook on TB management in children and adolescents is published alongside the WHO consolidated guidelines on TB. It includes evidence-based recommendations for the prevention and management of TB in these populations. 20. Surveillance data traditionally define children as individuals under 15 years of age. However, the consolidated guidelines and operational handbook define children as those under 10 years and adolescents as those aged 10–19 years. 21. Infants and young children, especially those under 2 years of age, are at higher risk of developing disseminated TB disease and TB meningitis, which are associated with high morbidity and mortality. 22. Adolescents face unique psychosocial challenges, requiring tailored support for adherence, autonomy, and transitioning from pediatric to adult health services. 23. The operational handbook aims to provide practical guidance for implementing WHO policy recommendations on TB prevention and management in children and adolescents under various programmatic circumstances and at different levels of the health system. 24. The handbook also supports countries in planning interventions to address the specific needs of children and adolescents with or at risk of TB, contributing to national efforts to build capacity among program managers and health workers. 25. The desired impact of WHO guidance on TB management in children and adolescents is to reduce TB morbidity and mortality in line with global targets, including the WHO End TB Strategy, the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, and the Political Declaration of the United Nations General Assembly High-level Meeting on TB. 26. To achieve these targets, multisectoral engagement, actions, and accountability are essential. 27. The handbook consolidates all recommendations related to TB prevention and management in children and adolescents into a single document, providing operational guidance for their implementation. 28. Recommendations are categorized as strong or conditional based on the balance of desirable and undesirable effects. Strong recommendations use the term should, while conditional recommendations use may. 29. The handbook includes practical tools, resources, and standard operating procedures to support TB management in children and adolescents. 30. The target audience for this handbook includes national TB programs, child health programs, pediatricians, health care workers, school health services, civil society organizations, and health care educators.
